items.title: What Alpine got right at Monza and everyone else got wrong
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The car that's currently sixth in the Formula 1 constructors' championship just took pole position in a straight fight in a dry qualifying session at the Italian Grand Prix.

F1 is used to freak underdog poles in mixed weather, but Pierre Gasly and Alpine's Monza achievement was something very different.

You have to go back to Pastor Maldonado's 2012 Spanish GP pole for Williams (then seventh in the championship) for an equivalent - and even that only happened because Lewis Hamilton's pole-winning McLaren was excluded from qualifying. Which means perhaps the real equivalent is Giancarlo Fisichella's 2009 Belgium pole for Force India (which was on zero points for the season before that race).

So how on earth did it happen?

The answer is really a 50/50 split between things Alpine got right and things the teams that should've beaten it got wrong.

What cost the favourite pole

Mercedes, and more specifically George Russell given team-mate Kimi Antonelli had a sizeable grid penalty, went into qualifying as the clear favourite, with most of Mercedes' rivals expecting Russell to emerge with pole position. 

And it was heading that way after the first Q3 run, with Russell on provisional pole, via a small tow assist on the start/finish straight from Antonelli, who had already made it clear he'd sacrifice his Q3 to help Russell.

But everything went wrong in the preparation for the crucial final lap. Russell was running on track behind Antonelli, however, Antonelli encountered a slowing Max Verstappen at Parabolica and had to back up into Russell, who also had to slow just before opening his flying lap.

Antonelli towed Russell on the start/finish straight, then jumped out of the way before the first chicane, leaving Russell to pick up a tow from Verstappen, albeit closer to him than he'd have liked. Russell called it a "bit of a mess". 

He still improved his laptime on his final run, but he ended up 0.060s behind Gasly - time he likely lost with the sub-optimal preparation. Plus, Russell struggled with his brakes locking like many drivers at Monza.

Russell admitted "It was a very scrappy session" and said the car didn't feel as good as it did in final practice.

It was undoubtedly still a car good enough to secure pole position. Put together Russell's three best sectors and his ideal lap is a 1m21.633s, 0.233s faster than his qualifying lap and 0.155s ahead of Gasly's pole lap.

Gasly in contrast put all of his three best sectors together on his final run.

Ferrari botched it but got away with it

If you contrast how smoothly Alpine ran throughout the three segments, getting Gasly at or near the top of the timesheet from Q1 right through to Q3, with Ferrari's relatively yo-yo performance, you can understand why Hamilton was so frustrated afterwards.

But for Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi oversteering through the middle of the Ascari chicane at the end of Q2, Hamilton wouldn't have even made Q3, and the higher risks taken by Ferrari (and McLaren for that matter) in trying to work both cars towards the front of the grid were more exposed to the ‘essentially sacrifice one car' approaches taken by Alpine, Mercedes and Red Bull.

And the fact Ferrari, even with its updated ADUO 2 engine, still carried a 10-20km/h deficit through every speed trap, suggested properly executed towing and clean laps were even more valuable to Hamilton's and Charles Leclerc's chances.

Considering how close Ferrari came to disaster in Q2, to then have both its cars ultimately (and fortuitously) starting on the second row of the grid is a fantastic outcome from such a messy session.

Monza was never expected to be McLaren territory, but the underlying pace of the MCL40 in qualifying trim was stronger than expected  - certainly far better than its final grid positions of sixth (Oscar Piastri) and eighth (Lando Norris).

"It would be a little bit of a red herring, or an excuse, to say 'oh we have too much drag," said team principal Andrea Stella of the role the car's aero efficiency weakness played. Instead, he pointed firmly in the direction of execution for McLaren's underachievement when it should have been "in the mix for the first couple of rows".

Hidden beneath a solid second and third in Q2 was the first key mistake. Piastri joined the track for his first run at the point where an out-of-synch Liam Lawson was on a quick lap, leading to him impeding the Red Bull in the chicane. A three-place grid penalty was the result, which puts Piastri sixth for tomorrow's race.

In Q3, there were myriad problems. McLaren struggled to position its cars ideally for a slipstream, which was partly owing to its position in the pitlane. This meant Norris didn't have a good slipstream on his first run in Q3. The McLarens were then at the front of the pack for the second run, with Piastri ahead, but when he locked up and cut the first chicane it not only hindered Norris but cost him his tow. Although Norris did improve on that run, it wasn't by anything like it should have been.

That lock-up from Piastri was a consequence of not optimising the outlaps by dealing well with the 4MJ harvest limit that makes it difficult to get temperature into everything before the start of a push lap. On top of that, Stella admitted that "we had some issues managing the battery, and here in Monza every 1% in the battery charge costs you a significant amount of milliseconds".

Red Bull had its own problems

In a way Red Bull made the biggest contribution to Alpine's pole given how much Verstappen's positioning affected the lap with which Russell really should've beaten Gasly.

And Red Bull should have been well placed to pull off some intra-team slipstreaming choreography given Lawson's grid penalties meant his own performance could be pretty much sacrificed to boost Verstappen.

Only if Lawson got to Q3, though. And thanks in large part (but not solely due) to Piastri baulking him in Q2 just as he was being given a reciprocal tow by Verstappen, Lawson wasn't actually there to play the team game when it was needed.

But Verstappen didn't think any of that mattered as much as the unspecified component failure that meant his Red Bull wasn't running at the right ride height for his Q3 runs.

"With how the car was responding in FP3, I didn't think I was fighting for pole, but it was quite a comfortable car to drive for once, and that was actually really nice," said Verstappen, "but unfortunately then we picked up another problem in qualifying."

Which was the diplomatic translation of his "this car is made of paper" radio rant after qualifying only sixth.

It is fair to say that Alpine was as surprised as its rivals about a pole position that it had never even dreamed of before the Italian Grand Prix weekend.

As it tried to piece together the answers on Saturday night as to how it had done it, it became clear that, as much as the big teams had all slipped up in their own ways, Alpine had equally got itself into the perfect position to capitalise by getting everything within its control spot on.

Having a Mercedes engine around Monza certainly helped, as it remains the benchmark power unit.

But one of Alpine's weaknesses earlier in the year – of not enough downforce – may well also have become a strength at Monza because of the low drag benefit.

The A526 appears to be very efficient with good top speed, so that helped lift it into contention.

The upgrades Gasly first got for Zandvoort have also served to give the car a better balance, and throughout practice Alpine had evolved the set-up to get him into a place he was very happy with.

That allowed him to attack the corners under braking (where others were struggling a lot) and take things to the edge through Ascari and Parabolica.

Perhaps most critical of all though was Gasly's perfect slipstream positioning in the train of cars. 

Alpine had confidence to drop to the back of the pack in that final run – as that offered the biggest tow gain.

That is not without risk, because there is a threat of slow traffic ahead meaning you don't get across the line in time (Gasly and Franco Colapinto made it with around 10 seconds to spare), plus a danger of anyone ahead going off and bringing out yellow flags that derail everything.

Despite a couple of cars going down the escape road at Turn 1, Gasly had a clear run and a beautiful slipstream from Hamilton ahead to secure himself the six-hundredths of a second edge that gave him the top spot over Russell.

items.title: Winners and losers from Italian Grand Prix F1 qualifying 2026
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Italian Grand Prix qualifying produced Formula 1’s most surprising dry weather polesitter in over a decade.

But apart from him, there weren’t many in the pitlane with reasons to be cheerful.

Here’s our winners and losers rundown.

Winner: Pierre Gasly and Alpine (1st)

A podium is worth 15 points and a pole is worth 'nothing' - Pierre Gasly has gained a pole and lost a podium in the span of this weekend, and yet it feels like the loss of 15 points is an acceptable trade for his F1 CV.

He's now an F1 winner and an F1 polesitter. That feels right. That feels significant. Regardless of what Sunday brings, he's poleman number 109 in F1's history books.

But it's also a big deal for Alpine, which has felt a bit no man's land-y for much of this season but seems to be squeezing out some good juice from its Zandvoort upgrade.

"I don't think we quite got the best out of the package in Zandvoort. It's a bit of a quirky circuit. But we've come here and the car is responding very well," an elated Steve Nielsen, Alpine's managing director, told Sky. 

"We got the gaps right. We got the tows right. The drivers didn't make a mistake. And laptime's clearly in the car. Because both cars were quite quick."

It's not the first midfield car to star on a low-downforce track, and it won't be the last, but compared to the rest of the season it feels even more significant than it usually would.

Loser: Max Verstappen (6th)

"This car is made out of paper," was a curious Q3 radio message from Max Verstappen, as the Red Bull’s habit of small but costly breakages continued with a problem that affected its ride height. Not ideal for this kerb-heavy circuit.

He felt that was far more significant than losing his slipstream wingman when Liam Lawson was eliminated in Q2 after coming across the slow-moving Oscar Piastri.

Speaking of which…

Loser: Oscar Piastri (3rd but penalised)

On pure qualifying results, Piastri was a ‘winner’ category candidate. Third on the grid at a track not great for the draggy McLaren, a long way ahead of team-mate Lando Norris and all despite (but also partly because of) blowing his last qualifying lap with a trip over the first chicane.

But already by that time a penalty was highly likely given Piastri’s inadvertent but massive block on Lawson in the middle of the first chicane in Q2. And, as referenced above, that Q3 error blew the lap on which he was supposed to be giving Norris a helpful tow.

So as third on the grid becomes sixth, that error and messing up the team’s plans means Piastri ends up in the Loser list instead.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (7th)

Given the championship leader spent all of Monza qualifying as team-mate Russell's tow servant, seventh in the actual results via one tow-less out of sequence solo lap that didn't matter was quite an achievement.

And one that probably suggests a) he'd have been a clear polesitter if he'd participated in qualifying properly and b) he has a shot at a very, very good result even from the back of the grid on Sunday.

One of his title rivals being beaten to pole by an Alpine and the other only qualifying fifth behind his team-mate and hinting at Ferrari team prioritisation angst already is quite good for Antonelli too on a weekend where he has nothing to lose.

Loser: Liam Lawson (14th)

Best-laid plans, and all that.

Red Bull hoped to use Lawson, faced as we now know with back-of-the-grid engine penalties, to tow Verstappen around in Q3. "But obviously you need to get there to be able to do it," reflected Lawson after his elimination, in 14th, in Q2.

That was much calmer than he'd been on the radio during the session. "Dude, what the f***?" he exclaimed as he was baulked by Piastri at the first chicane, which earned the McLaren driver a grid penalty, before telling Red Bull at the end of Q2: "Bro, that's actually appalling. I can't believe how badly you just left me out to f***ing dry!"

Maybe the Piastri block is what stopped him progressing. Maybe it wasn't; Lawson was three tenths away in the end, didn't improve in the final sector, and generally looked borderline - not helped by the fact he'd "spent the whole quali in clean air until that last lap".

"It was the first time I'd sat behind a car and the tyres were super hot," he said. "It just wasn't an ideal situation, so trying to do it for the first time was not ideal. But I think obviously having Oscar in Turn 1 probably hurt more than anything."

Whatever the cause(s), Lawson should really have been in the final part of qualifying.

Winner: Ollie Bearman (12th)

Having spent the last four months sliding backwards, Haas needed the upgrade it brought to Monza to show something encouraging.

So for Bearman to declare it "night-and-day different" and feel he had a shot at Q3 as he produced his best qualifying result since Shanghai in March will do nicely.

Bearman was also seven tenths of a second faster than team-mate Esteban Ocon. Only Bearman has the upgraded Ferrari engine, but he felt that was only a marginal difference and that he'd still have been fighting to get out of Q1 if that was the only change on the car for Monza.

Ocon has the same aero upgrades. Asked if they worked, he replied: "They worked on Ollie’s side".

Loser: Yuki Tsunoda (17th)

Tsunoda lost a lot of laptime on the straights and sounded totally bewildered by it, in comments that will sound familiar to anyone who's heard drivers up and down the grid speak about single-lap deployment and optimisation and all that jazz across 2026.

"I mean, if you look at the first sector, I was like seven tenths off - and there's only two corners," he mused. "I don't think I've done anything massively wrong, enough to lose a lot of laptime a lot in basically a straight line.

"I've done a lot of things in practice and it didn't happen like this."

His grid position is far from horrific - but, given that all of this is obviously part of a mission to prove his value to prospective F1 employers down the line, he's unlucky that what will surely be a short stand-in stint includes an energy-starved track like this, whether either a lack of experience with these cars' quirks or a freak deployment issue or both can really, really bite.

Winner: Valtteri Bottas (19th)

"It seems like we're on a better run. Things are working as they should. Like I said, it's also easy to find the rhythm when you can actually get laps with a car that works."

Bottas was talking about the execution of the weekend so far for his side of the Cadillac garage - "not really a single issue" - but his comments may as well apply to the wider picture of his season.

He's on a 6-0 run versus team-mate Sergio Perez in qualifyings, a significant reversal after a start to the season shaky enough on paper to where people started talking about potential replacements for 2027.

Perez had some issues through Q1 and didn't get the tow he would've liked - but also acknowledged Bottas put in a strong effort he "couldn't match".

For tomorrow, both still need to get through the opening stint - with Bottas worried about how the brakes will cope with running in traffic - but amid those continued teething problems for Cadillac things have certainly trended right for Bottas.

Loser: Aston Martin (21st + 22nd)

After the measured optimism the previous two rounds have offered, the Italian GP weekend has been a bruising reality check for Aston Martin-Honda so far.

OK, Fernando Alonso might've outqualified the two Cadillacs (and therefore possibly Alex Albon's Williams) had he made it out for a second run in Q1. Alonso certainly felt there was more laptime to come.

"We only did one set of tyres and the time we set was done with a scrubbed set, after waiting on the pitlane for a long time, cold tyres, etc.," he said. "So I think there was something more to come on the last attempt."

But the reason he didn't get to exploit it, and had to hop out of the car early before Q1 had ended? "The engine didn't start, so we had a problem with the power unit. I don't know if it's the ICE power or the battery or whatever it is, but yeah, it didn't start."

Sunday could be a long, lonely afternoon.

items.title: F1 2026 Italian GP starting grid with four penalties
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Italian Grand Prix qualifying threw up a real shock as Pierre Gasly and Alpine beat George Russell and Mercedes (and the rest of the Formula 1 frontrunners) to pole position.

But the starting grid wasn't quite set in stone come the end of Q3, as three grid penalties for engine component changes - for Kimi Antonelli, Alex Albon and Liam Lawson - were applied.

And there was a further change, too, as third-place qualifier Oscar Piastri received a three-place grid drop for impeding Lawson in Q2.

items.title: Hamilton's obvious frustration at Ferrari team tactics
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton believes his Ferrari Formula 1 team is putting its "dimming" chances of a 2026 title comeback at risk by not prioritising his campaign over team-mate Charles Leclerc's.

Hamilton trails championship leader Kimi Antonelli - who is starting at the back at Monza due to engine penalties - by 59 points and has 28 in hand over Leclerc.

He already felt last time out at Zandvoort that Ferrari's race execution didn't do enough to prioritise him as the driver ahead in the championship - contrasting it to how Mercedes played its cards with Antonelli and George Russell - and in qualifying at Monza saw another example of what he clearly sees as Ferrari leaving opportunities on the table.

There were a lot of knowing pauses as Hamilton recounted his session - in which he ultimately placed fifth, one spot behind Leclerc - and emphasised the importance of teamwork and the size of the deficit to Antonelli.

"I mean, we're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge - huge - deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed. So yeah, we do have to work as a team," he mused, before making his feelings clear with a couple of half-finished sentences: "Have we been...  if and when that would ever change... We'll find out, but all I can do is just try to arrive and do the best job I can."

Unrelated to the championship position, Hamilton has priority this weekend in terms of when he runs in qualifying relative to Leclerc - and naturally chose to go behind his team-mate, with slipstream more valuable here than at any other track.

Leclerc acknowledged this already on Thursday - but also said he didn't expect Ferrari to "compromise" his qualifying because of this, and indicated he would be happy to tow Hamilton along while himself having a rival car to get a slipstream from.

This appeared to be at the heart of what got Hamilton talking about championship position and priority on Saturday.

Though happy with his Ferrari, Hamilton was very close to missing the Q3 cut entirely - just 0.001s up on 11th-placed Gabriel Bortoleto in the end - and indicated his Q2 session was hindered by Leclerc's run plan preferences.

"We were supposed to do a push-cool-cool-push. But because everyone was waiting and Charles didn't want to go out first, we had to wait-wait-wait. And then we only got one push. And, yeah, it made it pretty challenging for us," he explained.

Q3 was then operationally suboptimal - he was supposed to be right behind Leclerc on both runs, but Ferrari didn't send him out early enough on run one - leaving him to run all by himself, a good third of the lap behind most of the grid.

"I didn't have any wheels on the car basically and everyone left whilst my engine was running.

"And that just put me out of rhythm [for the second run] because when you're following another car, when you're in that tow, you arrive much faster so the braking zones are different. And then when you're on your own, you lose the tows. A lot of time lost in the tows."

Asked about the conversations that have happened since Zandvoort in terms of teamwork and strategy, given his unhappiness there, Hamilton paused for a while - and didn't really answer the question in the end.

"What I can say is, Pierre [Gasly] did a great job of… clearly, looking from a distance, it looked like they [Alpine] worked really well as a team."

Asked by The Race whether Ferrari needs to throw its weight behind the lead driver given there remains a sniff of the title, he said: "There's light at the end of the tunnel, but it's getting dimmer the further we get through. Even though the team's doing an amazing job in bringing upgrades and pushing us forward, I'm so proud of everyone working- I say it all the time, but it's because I really am. I couldn't do what I do without seeing the great work of everybody, and I feel like I always want to make sure that I acknowledge them and recognise them for that, because I want them to continue to push and I want them to stay hungry and keep that passion and fire. 

"But also at the track, we need to come correct and act accordingly to make sure we get the result we need."

The issue, however, remains the same for Ferrari, which has Leclerc on an even longer-term contract now and would strain to make the case to the Monegasque that it's already time to give up on his title hopes in favour of Hamilton's.

A total of 283 points should remain up for grabs in F1 this season, which Leclerc can argue should be sufficient for him to stay in the hunt, too - especially as he and Hamilton have been virtually indistinguishable in terms of the qualifying head-to-head this year.

items.title: Piastri gets grid penalty for Lawson Q2 incident
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Oscar Piastri has lost third-place on the grid for Formula 1’s Italian Grand Prix after impeding Liam Lawson in qualifying.

Towards the end of Q2, the McLaren driver exited the pits on an out-lap just as the Red Bull duo of Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were beginning their final push laps.

The Red Bulls were running out of sync with the field as Lawson had towed Verstappen initially and Verstappen was trying to help Lawson get through to Q3 by returning the favour.

Piastri managed to get out of the way of Verstappen, but as Piastri turned into the first chicane he baulked Lawson, who lost valuable time that he was unable to recover later in the lap.

Piastri was summoned to see the stewards after qualifying, and explained that while had been warned about the Red Bull duo approaching, he was not aware they were on push laps.

When he realised that Verstappen was indeed going for a time, he got out of the way as best he could.

However, due to his positioning, he had no choice but to continue to roll into the chicane where he impeded Lawson.

Although the stewards accepted that Piastri had been left in a tricky spot, they felt that there was no option but to serve him with a penalty for blocking a rival.

A statement issued by the FIA said: “The Stewards accept that with the information he had, and the situation he was placed in, the driver of Car 81 had, at this stage, no other options available and hence, inadvertently, and also unnecessarily, impeded Car 30.

“Therefore the standard penalty of a drop of 3 grid positions is imposed.”

The penalty drops Piastri from third down to sixth, and means that Ferrari duo Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton will move up to the second row behind Pierre Gasly and George Russell.

Lawson’s failure to get through to Q3 meant that Verstappen was left alone to try to find a slipstream, with the team having hoped that Lawson could act as support in helping give his team-mate a tow thanks to the engine change penalty that puts him to the back of the grid for Sunday's race.

items.title: Gasly and Alpine stun Mercedes to take Italian GP pole
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Pierre Gasly claimed a shock pole position for the Alpine Formula 1 team in Italian Grand Prix qualifying at Monza, beating George Russell's Mercedes to the top spot.

The recently upgraded Alpine looked top-10 fast through practice but no one was expecting it to be a pole threat come qualifying.

Yet Gasly was super quick from the earliest runs in Q1, where he was fastest of all and team-mate Franco Colapinto was fourth.

Q2 was slightly tougher, where Gasly ended up fourth behind Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes and the two McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris, while Colapinto slipped to eighth.

But in the top-10 shootout Gasly came back into the picture, lapping just 0.071s behind Russell's Mercedes on the first Q3 runs, and placing third behind Piastri's McLaren.

And on the final runs, even though Russell found 0.083s thanks to a tow from Max Verstappen, Gasly found more by following a Ferrari to claim his first pole position in F1 by 0.06s.

Piastri locked up at the first chicane on his final Q3 run, but his first lap was still good enough for third - though questions remain as to whether he may be penalised for impeding Liam Lawson's Red Bull in Q2.

The Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were fourth and fifth, after narrowly avoiding Q2 elimination, where Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi almost eliminated Hamilton and was only 0.008s slower than Leclerc.

Verstappen's Red Bull rounded out the top six, ahead of championship leader Antonelli, who sacrificed his Q3 to aid Russell's pole bid.

Antonelli will drop to the back of the grid thanks to taking a new engine for this weekend.

Colapinto was eighth in the second Alpine, ahead of Norris, whose final Q3 lap was compromised by Piastri's Turn 1 lock-up - robbing Norris of a lap-long tow.

Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10 for Racing Bulls, just 0.03s down on the 2025 world champion.

Bortoleto missed out on Q3, just 0.001s down on Hamilton's Ferrari, ruing a slide in the middle of the Ascari chicane, but he will anyway start 10th thanks to Antonelli's grid penalty.

Ollie Bearman's Haas, Nico Hulkenberg's Audi, the compromised Red Bull of Lawson, the Williams of Carlos Sainz and Esteban Ocon's Haas were the other cars eliminated in Q2.

In Q1 it was Yuki Tsunoda's Racing Bulls and Alex Albon's Williams that joined the expected Cadillacs and Aston Martin-Hondas in being eliminated.

Tsunoda was told to calm down on team radio after the session, while Albon was thanked by Williams for helping tow Sainz into Q2.

Valtteri Bottas was only 0.008s slower than Albon's Williams in the battle at the back, where Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin, which didn't make a second run in Q1, was more than half a second slower than Sergio Perez's Cadillac as energy-starved Monza brutally exposed the upgraded Honda engine's remaining power shortfall.

items.title: Russell fastest in final Italian GP practice
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell marked himself out as favourite for Italian Grand Prix pole position by setting the pace in final practice at Monza.

Russell and team-mate Kimi Antonelli spent part of the session practicing the tows that are likely to play a significant role in the fight for pole position in qualifying, though Russell looked fast with and without assistance.

His final effort - a 1m22.219s that was three tenths clear of Friday's FP2 benchmark - came without a tow from Antonelli (who has grid penalties this weekend) and was 0.226s faster than the next-best time, set by Lewis Hamilton.

Max Verstappen was third as Red Bull's single-lap pace appeared in a much better place than on Friday, though he and Ferrari driver Hamilton did have a minor on-track altercation at the end of FP3 that was noted by the stewards.

Hamilton jumped ahead of Verstappen entering the Alboreto (Parabolica) corner, with Verstappen subsequently giving Hamilton a thumbs-up as they crossed the start/finish line to indicate his lap had been compromised and then running deep into the first corner to ensure Hamilton could not take the apex.

Championship leader Antonelli was fourth ahead of Lando Norris, the winner of the past two races, in the best of the McLarens.

His team-mate Oscar Piastri set the fastest first sector of all on his final attempt and was still inside Russell's benchmark through sector two, but ended the lap more than half a second down and only eighth-fastest - a clear indication of the varying energy deployment patterns teams are working to this weekend.

Between them were Charles Leclerc in the second Ferrari and the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad, who for a while at the end of the session held the fastest final sector courtesy of a huge tow from the Audi of Nico Hulkenberg.

That partly accounted for Lindblad's gap to the next-best midfield driver, Pierre Gasly, who finished the session ahead of team-mate Franco Colapinto as the Alpine duo rounded out the top 10.

Liam Lawson had a difficult start to Saturday in the second Red Bull, looping his RB22 as he got on the power - and the kerb - through the first chicane. He finished the session in 12th, the best part of a second off Russell and more than six tenths down on Verstappen.

At the back, Fernando Alonso improved late on to lead the Aston Martin-Cadillac quartet that once again looks cut adrift.

items.title: F2 reveals revised car to reflect F1 2026 changes
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Formula 2 has revealed a heavily modified car for the coming seasons at the Italian Grand Prix, bringing it closer to the look of Formula 1's current machine.

The revised car, which will retain the existing chassis, was revealed in the F1 paddock at Monza on Saturday and will be used in F1's primary feeder series from 2027 to 2029.

F2 last introduced a new car in 2024 to more closely mirror the look of F1's ground-effect-era cars used from 2022-25.

This new 2027 car better reflects the visual direction of F1's new 2026 cars but without being a complete overhaul, keeping costs lower.

Its aero package is also designed to allow cars to follow each other more closely.

The new car will be powered by the same 3.4-litre turbocharged V6 Mecachrome engine used in the 2024-26 generation.

And it will run on 18-inch wheelrims once more, having pioneered them on its 2020 car, two years before F1 adopted them.

The car will run on sustainable fuel, supplied by Aramco, partner of Aston Martin's F1 team.

For the first time, the car will feature an on-board starter, meaning stalled cars are less likely to be stranded.

F2 said this had been accomplished through the development of "an evolution of the current gearbox" from supplier Hewland.

It should be the car used by Lando Norris's brand-new LN4 Fusion team next year, led by former Prema leader Rene Rosin.

The team is yet to be officially granted an entry, but this is believed to be a formality.

items.title: Briatore-FIA row continues with appeal court response
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
The FIA International Court of Appeal has issued a statement defending its processes in the wake of Alpine Formula 1 executive advisor Flavio Briatore's comments that appeared to question the independence of one judge on its panel.

Briatore started a public row against McLaren during a press conference appearance at the Italian Grand Prix on Friday. That came after the FIA communicated that its International Court of Appeal had ruled to reinstate the two five-second penalties that Pierre Gasly incurred at the Monaco GP in June, which Alpine had previously successfully had quashed.

This meant Gasly lost his podium for a second time, having crossed the line in third.

While Briatore said he accepted the decision, he also appeared to question the impartiality of one of the four ICA judges - Filippo Marchino - on the panel during the August hearing.

Reading from a piece of paper that he continued to refer to, Briatore claimed Marchino had been "very nasty during the hearing" and was "acting as a prosecutor".

"And after, we found out what is the reason why he's so nasty, this guy? He's very linked with McLaren. I'm very surprised this guy has the link with McLaren," Briatore said.

That McLaren mention is pertinent because it was one of two teams, alongside Red Bull, that had appealed the decision to reinstate Gasly to third place.

In a statement released on Saturday morning, the FIA Court of Appeal rejected any suggestion that the process of its selection of judges had not been impartial.

It did not name Briatore directly but said the comments related to case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09 - the hearing for the case brought by McLaren and Red Bull.

"The FIA courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the IBA guidelines on conflicts of interest in international arbitration," the FIA statement read.

"All judges are elected by the FIA general assemblies, some of them upon proposition of a group of at least five F1 teams in accordance with the FIA statutes.

"They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA judicial and disciplinary rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA compliance officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties."

The International Court of Appeal has a roster of 36 leading legal experts, at least eight of whom are selected to be part of a pool that can be picked for each case.

This pool is communicated to relevant parties ahead of time to assess whether there are any "serious and objective reasons to consider that any or all of the shortlisted judges should be recused due to the existence of a conflict of interest or other legitimate grounds".

The statement said this had happened, with the relevant parties "invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the court".

"None did so," the statement added. "No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.

"The ICA emphasises the importance of constituting panels with judges from different cultural and geographical backgrounds. This helps ensure that the deliberations and discussions reflect a diversity of legal traditions, perspectives and approaches, further strengthening the fairness, independence, credibility of the process and access to a fair trial.

"A court's decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges. The court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges. The FIA courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process."

items.title: What F1 teams' Monza deployment patterns have revealed
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 cars are at their most energy-starved at Monza since the in-season rule changes were agreed in April, and there are currently plenty of telling differences in energy deployment between the cars.

Teams - particularly manufacturers and their customers - often converge closer on energy deployment come qualifying, with more variance on Friday.

But there's still some interesting patterns we can see from analysing the data, the long run times and what the teams and drivers have said so far at the Italian Grand Prix.

Ferrari has the benefit of its upgraded 'ADUO 2' power unit this weekend but, given the team's played down how big a step it is, there's no reason to believe Mercedes still doesn't have the benchmark 2026 power unit.

Russell vs Leclerc fastest FP2 times

Looking at the GP Tempo data of George Russell's FP2-topping time (green) and Charles Leclerc's best (red; 0.120 seconds slower), you can see the Ferrari loses time to the Mercedes on the first three straights, to the point where Leclerc is 0.466s adrift on the entry to Ascari.

It's out of Ascari and towards the Parabolica (Alboreto corner) where Ferrari claws back most of that time - an interesting deployment split that, if maintained, would certainly make lap one on Sunday exciting. And you can add to that, as Alex Albon pointed out on Thursday, that "the Ferraris tend to be quite opportunistic in [the opening laps]; they run different modes, and they can catch other cars out".

How strong is the upgraded Ferrari engine?

Comparing the Haas drivers does give you an unusual opportunity to assess the upgraded Ferrari power unit as Ollie Bearman has it and team-mate Esteban Ocon doesn't.

Though that does come with the caveat that Ocon was suffering from the parts inconsistency issues that have hurt Haas all season.

Those inconsistencies often result in a loss of downforce or feeling that will certainly explain a lot of Ocon's one-second deficit to Bearman - who was eighth fastest in FP2.

But the straightline speed difference between Bearman (purple) and Ocon (white) is noticeable on the run to both Ascari and into the Parabolica.

Bearman vs Ocon fastest FP2 times

Really, we'd need those parts inconsistencies to be solved to know the true difference in power units.

Certainly Haas's aero upgrade (which is on both cars) is performing well with what Bearman described as "the best Friday" since March.

That's sorely needed as Haas has long drifted outside of points-scoring contention, having not scored at the six rounds since Monaco in June.

McLaren's expectations of a tough Monza look correct based on its Friday performance, where Lando Norris was almost four tenths off Russell on single lap pace, and slightly further away on long-run pace.

McLaren’s technical director for engineering Neil Houldey said: "From an energy perspective, we've still got a bit of work to do.

"There's certainly laptime there available to us, a little bit moving around recharge, moving around deployment."

The GP Tempo data certainly supports that when you compare Russell (green) and Norris (papaya).

Even with the same power unit, McLaren is losing out on the three long straights after Turn 1 - with the run to Parabolica particularly painful.

We have seen plenty of times this year quite different energy deployment strategies between Mercedes and customer McLaren on Friday, before McLaren learns and starts to converge by qualifying.

McLaren did successfully run the modified version of what it's dubbing its "H-wing", with "no reason to take it off" unless the team has suddenly found something wrong in the data overnight.

Norris summarised: "We'll see what we can change overnight, but we're not in as good a position compared to the last few weekends, so, yeah, tough."

Its shorter gear ratios won't be helping it here either. It knows it pitched them wrong this year, but it doesn't want to use its one joker to change them (as Audi has) because of the cost, which could instead go to aerodynamic upgrades.

Red Bull is in a similar position and will have needed a fruitful overnight period if it's to have any chance of joining the Mercedes/Ferrari fight. The only silver lining for the team was Verstappen's solid long run where he was only three tenths off the Mercedes, which probably underpins technical director Pierre Wache's hope that a podium is still possible if Red Bull takes a step forward overnight.

Honda's 'Spec 2' is still lacking

This is the worst-case scenario circuit for Aston Martin-Honda, given its sizeable power unit deficit - one that its upgraded 'Spec 2' engine hasn't solved.

Looking at Fernando Alonso's best FP2 lap versus midfield leader Arvid Lindblad's, there are clear major losses on every straight.

Alonso loses four tenths on the run to Turn 1 alone and a whopping half a second from exiting Ascari to Parabolica.

Honda's chief engineer Shintaro Orihara said: "As we can see from the results, our straightline speed isn't enough compared to our competitors.

"This isn't a surprise, and we knew this was coming at a circuit where the power unit performance is so important.

"Therefore, this track presents a challenge for us. We will optimise our settings to maximise our performance as much as possible, but we should remain realistic for what’s to come."

What's to come is likely a fight with Cadillac and potentially Williams to avoid returning to the back of the grid this weekend after the Zandvoort ninth-place watermark.

As expected, the GPS data of a single lap around Monza looks very different to one year ago.

There's a night-and-day difference when you look at Norris's FP2-topping time from 2025 (orange) versus Russell's 2026 FP2 benchmark (green) - with 2.681s between them.

Norris 2025 FP2 vs Russell 2026 FP2

There's a sizeable difference in-between the Lesmos and on the run to Ascari, Parabolica, and the finish line.

There isn't the dramatic tail-off in speed that we saw prior to the in-season rule changes at the end of the straights, but rather a levelling off where they lose a lot of time versus one year ago.

On Thursday, Oscar Piastri said the speeds at the end of the straights in Monza in the pre-weekend simulations were slower than they were in Hungary - and that's proved to be the case on Friday, with Russell 6km/h quicker by the end of Turn 1 in Hungary than at the end of any of the Monza straights.

Given Pirelli is expecting Sunday's race to be an easy one-stop with tyre degradation minimal on Friday, differing energy deployment/harvesting strategies will once again be a critical factor.

items.title: The early verdict on Ferrari's Italian GP engine upgrade
items.author: Edd Straw
items.content:
Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur always downplays the impact of specific upgrade packages, so by his standards his verdict after the debut of the upgraded Formula 1 power unit was encouraging despite confirming it's still at a deficit on power.

With Charles Leclerc second fastest in FP2, 0.120s slower than pacesetting Mercedes driver George Russell, and showing promising long-run pace, there was nothing on Friday to suggest that Ferrari had taken a giant leap to the front. What there was is proof of gains with the second engine upgrade introduced under the FIA’s Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) regulations, the first having arrived in Austria in late June.

"You have to keep in mind the performance in the straight line is the drag, the weight of the car, it's everything, it's not just the engine," said Vasseur. "We did a step for sure, and we didn't bring ADUO 2 for nothing, but I think we still have a decent gap."

What Lewis Hamilton calls a "considerable" deficit to Mercedes was evident on the straights. Comparing Leclerc's fastest FP2 lap to Russell's, there is a clear pattern of the Ferrari losing ground on the straights but making gains on the brakes and through the corners.

He loses around six tenths in the first two-thirds of the lap before clawing back a couple of those on the final straight, with Russell suffering more clipping on the run to Parabolica. In line with the comments of many teams and drivers, there's still plenty of room for optimisation of the harvesting and deployment strategies on this energy-starved track.

While Hamilton complained about the balance that made it "really hard to pull the lap out of the car" and "not an easy one to drive" after some set-up changes in FP2, he was hopeful that there are gains to come both in terms of set-up and the energy management.

"That's what we need to look into, if it's that [or] if it's the deployment," said Hamilton when asked if there could be gains in trimming back the downforce and therefore drag.

"But the engine is an improvement, which I'm really grateful for the guys back at the factory for working on. But our deployment schedule is different to the others, our competitors. It seems like they maybe have less drag for the straights, so that's something we need to definitely look at."

Hamilton also described the engine as "really nice to drive in the low speed". But it was Leclerc who led the way for Ferrari not only on single-lap pace but the long runs.

His long run was just three hundredths a lap on average off Kimi Antonelli's, albeit with the significant caveat that Leclerc was on the softs and the Mercedes on the hards. Despite that offset, that potentially puts Ferrari as the closest challenger, albeit with most expecting Mercedes to have the edge depending on how overnight changes shift the balance of power.

The wildcard in this is Red Bull, with Max Verstappen complaining of balance problems and playing catch-up after sitting out FP1 to allow Ayumu Iwasa to run.

"Clearly we have a balance issue on the car," said Red Bull technical director Pierre Wache. "A little bit like Zandvoort, to be honest, and we try to understand what the issue is, try to fix it in a different way by setup and car components.

"It's the main thing we are working on. What doesn't help is when Max didn’t drive during FP1 and he jumped in the car there, we have less time to react and now we have to react for FP3."

And yet, in the other Red Bull, Liam Lawson - whose preparation was complicated by having to put in the pre-weekend legwork both for his current team and Racing Bulls amid uncertainty about Isack Hadjar's fitness - produced an impressively quick and consistent hard stint that matched Antonelli's. However, both Leclerc and Antonelli encountered traffic during their stint, potentially slightly flattering Red Bull.

As for McLaren, Lando Norris was 0.443s off on the long runs, with his completed on hards, and only a little closer at 0.384s off on overall pace on a day he called "much trickier than the last few Fridays".

"It's a bit everywhere, honestly," said Norris, winner of the previous two grands prix, of the time loss. "There's not one corner we're quicker than anyone else ahead of us.

"We're losing a bit in the straights compared to Mercedes, which we kind of expect, but also the high speed is where we lose most of our laptime, which is normally where we're quick. So we have to try and figure out a few things, but we're just off the pace everywhere at the minute."

In the midfield battle, Arvid Lindblad led the way on a strong day for Racing Bulls, but unusually with Haas's Ollie Bearman just 0.021s behind. The Haas pace slipped behind Racing Bulls and Alpine (with Franco Colapinto delighted with the car in FP1 but finding the car "disconnected" in FP2) on the long runs, but this was nonetheless encouraging.

Both Haas VF-26s are running a major aerodynamic upgrade, but only Bearman has the upgraded Ferrari engine (Haas just has one available this weekend), with team principal Ayao Komatsu confirming "it's delivering in terms of characteristics". That's encouraging for a team that has not scored in the last six events, but less positive is the ongoing "inconsistency issues" that have hit both cars at times recently with Esteban Ocon having problems.

Audi, which introduced no aerodynamic upgrades on Friday but played the joker allowing changes to the homologated gear ratios/final drive, struggled compared to the midfield leaders a little more than expected, with an improvement expected on Saturday. That left it only just ahead of on single-lap pace, and a fraction behind on long-run pace, Carlos Sainz's soft-shod Williams, which had an experimental Friday while making the most of its time before the major upgrade due in Azerbaijan later this month.

At the back, an intriguing early-season subplot returned with Aston Martin struggling as anticipated despite the introduction of the upgraded Honda engine at Zandvoort two weeks ago.

There were at least driveability improvements as hoped, something Lance Stroll described as "a little bit better", but the fact that Valtteri Bottas reckoned Cadillac "have the upper hand on the straights" means a repeat of Fernando Alonso's Zandvoort points-scoring heroics seems unlikely.

items.title: What's next after Briatore's press conference bombshell
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Alpine executive advisor Flavio Briatore stirred up one of the most explosive Formula 1 press conferences of recent times on Friday amid the fall out of the FIA International Court of Appeal verdict that took away his team's Monaco Grand Prix podium.

Just a few hours after the FIA published the verdict that McLaren and Red Bull's had been successful in their appeal against Pierre Gasly having his Monte Carlo top-three finish reinstated, Briatore went on the offensive.

But rather than criticise the conclusions the judges had come to, he took aim at one of them in particular in suggesting that he had links with McLaren.

"Filippo Marchino is a judge, he was very nasty during the hearing, was acting as a prosecutor," said Briatore as he read off a piece of paper in his hand.

"And after, we found out what is the reason why so nasty, this guy. He is very linked with McLaren."

Briatore said that he felt the situation was "very unfair".

He added "we have a nice picture of this guy at a speech for McLaren in 2018 in MSO, Beverly Hills", although without showing the piece of paper.

"He has a foundation, it's called One Drop Foundation, and McLaren gave two, three McLaren cars," Briatore added. "This was quite unfair."

This remark about the cars specifically is linked to a charity auction that was held in 2019 for the One Drop Foundation, of which Marchino sits on the board of directors.

One Drop was created by Guy Laliberte, the co-founder of Cirque du Soleil, who has long had ties to McLaren as a friend of former McLaren supremo Ron Dennis.

So, there is clear logic in it obtaining items from McLaren as part of the charity auction that Briatore referenced.

Briatore's remarks not only took the FIA and the media present by surprise, but they clearly infuriated McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, who gave an angry response to suggestions that there was anything untoward at play.

"I find that this conference going in this direction is quite insulting for McLaren, for the reputation of a team that deserves a lot of respect," said Stella.

"If anybody makes these kind of allegations - which seem quite serious - they are going to have to take the responsibility for what they are saying in a public forum.

"The hearing, the whole International Court of Appeal, was conducted to the highest standards and we should not question this phase like it’s been done."

Briatore suggested that the matter was not closed though, as he hinted that Alpine might considering taking the matter further.

"We’ve been thinking about it," he said. "Just pass the weekend and after that we think about it. For the moment, I don’t know."

Quite what Alpine's options could be is unclear, because the FIA's International Court of Appeal is the highest authority - and parties cannot appeal what it decides.

However, there is a right of review element that is similar to normal stewards' verdicts where decisions can be challenged if any "important new evidence is discovered which was unknown at the outset of the case before the ICA".

Briatore suggested Alpine knew nothing about the alleged links until after the hearing.

"We found out, after the meeting, logically, not before," he said. "We found out this guy was linked with the McLaren team."

It is unclear if what Briatore said is new information would be enough to cross the threshold for a right of review, because the FIA made clear on Friday that the make-up of the judging panel is put through a strong vetting process.

The International Court of Appeal has a roster of 36 leading legal experts, with at least eight of them selected to be part of a pool that can be picked for each case.

This pool is communicated to relevant parties well ahead of time to see if there are any "serious and objective reasons to consider that any or all of the shortlisted judges should be recused due to the existence of a conflict of interest or other legitimate grounds".

At no point in this process did Alpine offer any objection about who the shortlisted judges were, and that meant the president of the ICA - Monaco's Laurent Anselmi - went ahead and selected four for the hearing.

Interestingly, as part of F1's regulations, at least one of the judges involved in an ICA hearing that relates to the world championship must have been elected to the pool at the FIA's general assembly on proposal from at least five teams or three manufacturers.

Back in 2023, Marchino (as well as Luigi Fumagalli, who was also a judge in the Monaco appeal hearing) was nominated at the FIA's general assembly after being proposed by teams.

Any judges proposed by teams are subject to a due diligence check by the FIA compliance officer, and are then reviewed by an ad hoc panel before recommendations are made to the eligibility assessment committee.

Beyond this initial assessment, when judges are called up to specific cases they must confirm to the FIA's secretary general that they are not affected by any conflict of interest.

Only once this is complete will the final make-up of the ICA judging panel be finalised, with it then kept secret from everyone involved in the case until the day of the hearing.

With the hearing finished and the ICA verdict now out, the F1 paddock must wait a little longer to see if a three-month fight over the Monaco GP podium is prolonger further still.
